guides.title: History of Apple Inc.
guides.summary: The story of Apple from the 1976 garage startup through the Apple II, the Macintosh, near-bankruptcy in the 1990s, the return of Steve Jobs, the iPod and iPhone revolutions, and the Tim Cook era of services and Apple silicon.

sections.heading: The Garage Years: Jobs, Wozniak, and the Apple I
sections.body:
Apple Computer Company was founded on April 1, 1976, by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne, in the Santa Clara Valley of California just as that region was acquiring its new name, Silicon Valley. The two Steves had met years earlier through a mutual friend and bonded over electronics and pranks; both had attended Homestead High School in Cupertino, and both had worked in the local industry, Wozniak at Hewlett-Packard designing calculators and Jobs at the video game company Atari. Their first commercial collaboration, before Apple, was a blue box, an illegal device for placing free long-distance phone calls, which they built and sold to students; Jobs later said there would have been no Apple without the blue boxes, because they proved the pair could build something and sell it.

The technical founder was Wozniak. A member of the Homebrew Computer Club, the legendary hobbyist gathering that met at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center auditorium beginning in 1975, Wozniak wanted a computer of his own and could not afford the Altair 8800 that had ignited the hobby. So he designed one around the inexpensive MOS Technology 6502 microprocessor, which sold for about 25 dollars when Intel chips cost far more. His machine was radical in its economy: a complete working computer on a single circuit board that could drive a television as a display and take input from a typewriter-style keyboard, at a time when most hobby machines communicated through toggle switches and blinking lights. Wozniak gave the schematics away freely at Homebrew meetings, in the hacker spirit of the club. Jobs saw something different: people who admired the design but lacked the skill or patience to build it would pay for an assembled board.

That insight became the Apple I, priced with Wozniak puckish humor at 666.66 dollars. The decisive early sale came from Paul Terrell, owner of the Byte Shop in Mountain View, one of the first computer retail stores anywhere, who ordered fifty machines at 500 dollars each, but only if they arrived fully assembled. The founders scraped together parts on thirty days of credit, and the assembly line was the Jobs family home on Crist Drive in Los Altos, first a bedroom and then the famous garage, with Jobs sister Patty and friends inserting chips at a kitchen-table wage. They delivered on time, paid their suppliers, and were in business. Roughly 200 Apple I units were built in total; a few dozen survive, and working examples have sold at auction for hundreds of thousands of dollars, one exceeding 900,000.

Ronald Wayne, the forgotten third founder, was a colleague of Jobs from Atari, brought in at age 41 to be the adult in the room; he drew the first Apple logo, an ornate engraving of Isaac Newton under an apple tree, wrote the partnership agreement, and held ten percent of the company. Twelve days later, worried that as the only partner with personal assets he was exposed to the company debts, he sold his stake back for 800 dollars, later accepting about 1,500 more to relinquish all claims. Had he kept his ten percent, it would eventually have been worth hundreds of billions. Wayne always maintained he made the best decision with the information he had, and his story became Silicon Valley favorite cautionary tale about equity and risk. By the end of 1976, Jobs and Wozniak were designing a far more ambitious machine, and the garage operation was about to meet professional capital.

sections.heading: The Apple II and the Personal Computer Boom
sections.body:
The machine that made Apple a real company was the Apple II, unveiled at the West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco in April 1977 and shipped that June at 1,298 dollars for the base model with 4 kilobytes of memory. Where the Apple I had been a bare board for hobbyists, the Apple II was a finished consumer product: a friendly beige plastic case designed by Jerry Manock at Jobs insistence, an integrated keyboard, and, thanks to a Wozniak circuit design of legendary cleverness, color graphics driven from a home television, something no rival offered at the price. It arrived alongside two other 1977 machines aimed at ordinary buyers, the Commodore PET and the Tandy TRS-80, a trio the press later called the holy trinity of the personal computer revolution, but the Apple II outlived and outsold its classmates by years. It had eight internal expansion slots, a decision Wozniak fought Jobs to keep, which spawned an industry of add-on cards, and in 1978 it gained the Disk II floppy drive, another Wozniak masterpiece that used software to replace most of the expensive controller hardware, making Apple floppy storage both better and cheaper than competitors.

Professional money and management arrived with the product. Mike Markkula, a marketing manager who had retired from Intel at 32 wealthy from stock options, was introduced to the founders in late 1976, saw the plan, and invested 250,000 dollars, of which 80,000 was equity and the rest a loan, for roughly a third of the company. Markkula was arguably the most consequential early decision-maker after the founders themselves: he wrote the company first business plan, drafted its three-point marketing philosophy of empathy, focus, and impute, personally guaranteed credit lines, recruited Michael Scott as the company first president in February 1977, and taught Jobs, then 21, how business worked. Apple Computer was incorporated on January 3, 1977, absorbing the old partnership.

The transformative event for sales came from outside: software. In 1979, Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston, working from a Harvard Business School idea, released VisiCalc, the first electronic spreadsheet, and released it first and only on the Apple II for a critical year. VisiCalc was the original killer application, a program so valuable that people bought the computer just to run it; accountants and small business owners who had never touched a computer walked into dealers asking for VisiCalc and left with an Apple II. Sales curves bent upward: Apple sold roughly 2,500 Apple II machines in 1977, 8,000 in 1978, and 35,000 in 1979, with revenue climbing from under a million dollars toward 47 million in fiscal 1979 and 117 million in 1980.

The Apple II also planted Apple in education, a stronghold the company held for two decades. Through programs like the 1983 Kids Cannot Wait initiative, which donated roughly 9,000 computers to California schools with the help of a state tax incentive, and aggressive courting of teachers and districts, the Apple II became the standard American classroom computer, running educational software like Oregon Trail for a generation of students. The product line itself proved astonishingly durable: the II Plus of 1979, the IIe of 1983, the compact IIc of 1984, and the 16-bit IIGS of 1986 carried the family forward until the last IIe rolled off the line in November 1993, a sixteen-year run. Well into the Macintosh era, the Apple II remained the company profit engine, a fact often forgotten in the mythology; it was Wozniak elegant, open, expandable machine that paid for everything that came next.

sections.heading: Going Public: The 1980 IPO and the New Silicon Valley Wealth
sections.body:
Apple initial public offering on December 12, 1980, was the largest since the Ford Motor Company had gone public in 1956, and it announced to the general public that a new industry had arrived. Underwritten by Morgan Stanley and the boutique technology bank Hambrecht and Quist, the offering priced 4.6 million shares at 22 dollars each. Demand overwhelmed supply: the stock opened at 25.87 and finished its first trading day around 29 dollars, valuing the four-year-old company at approximately 1.8 billion dollars, more than Ford itself at the time and roughly the valuation of established industrial firms that had taken half a century to build. The sale raised over 100 million dollars for the company, war chest money for the product gambles of the coming decade. Massachusetts regulators, applying old blue-sky investor protection rules, considered the offering so speculative that they barred individual investors in the state from buying shares at the open, a restriction that reads today as a museum piece.

The IPO minted wealth on a scale Silicon Valley had not seen. An estimated 300 people, employees and early investors, became millionaires that morning, said at the time to be more than any single company had created in one event. Steve Jobs, holding about 15 percent, was suddenly worth on the order of 250 million dollars at age 25; Steve Wozniak roughly half that; Mike Markkula 250,000 dollar bet of 1977 had multiplied a thousandfold. Wozniak, characteristically, felt the distribution was unjust: before the offering he had personally sold or transferred shares at low prices to dozens of rank-and-file employees who had been excluded from options, in what became known as the Woz Plan. The IPO also fixed the template for Valley ambition: stock options as the currency of recruitment, the public offering as the finish line that turned engineers into millionaires, a social technology arguably as influential as anything Apple shipped.

Behind the triumphant offering, the company was navigating turbulence. The Apple III, launched in May 1980 as the business-oriented successor to the II, was the company first major failure: rushed to market with a case designed before the electronics, chronically unreliable, initially without a cooling fan because Jobs forbade one, it suffered failure rates so high that early units were infamously prescribed a lift-and-drop to reseat loose chips. Around 120,000 were sold against far grander hopes, and the III was quietly discontinued by 1984. In February 1981, Wozniak crashed his Beechcraft Bonanza on takeoff, suffering injuries and amnesia; during his long recuperation he stepped back from engineering, returned to Berkeley to finish his degree under a pseudonym, and bankrolled two rock festivals, never again playing a central product role. That same month brought Black Wednesday, when president Michael Scott abruptly fired around forty employees; Scott himself was eased out soon after, with Markkula becoming president and Jobs chairman.

Competitive weather was changing too. In August 1981, IBM, the most powerful company in the computer industry, released its Personal Computer, the IBM PC, built from off-the-shelf parts with an operating system licensed from a small company called Microsoft. Apple greeted it with a cocky full-page advertisement in the Wall Street Journal reading Welcome, IBM. Seriously. The confidence was misplaced: corporate America trusted IBM, the PC open architecture invited an army of clone makers, and within three years the IBM standard, not Apple, defined business computing. Apple answer to that challenge was already gestating in two secret projects named after apples, Lisa and Macintosh, and in a technology Jobs had glimpsed at a Xerox research center in December 1979.

sections.heading: Xerox PARC, the Lisa, and the Road to the Macintosh
sections.body:
The ideas that defined Apple next decade were not invented at Apple. They came from Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, PARC, where through the 1970s researchers led by figures like Alan Kay, Butler Lampson, and Chuck Thackeray had built the Alto, a machine organized around a bitmapped screen displaying windows, icons, and menus, driven by a pointing device called a mouse, invented earlier by Douglas Engelbart at SRI and famously demonstrated in 1968. The Alto was networked by Ethernet, printed to laser printers, and ran object-oriented software in Smalltalk; it was, functionally, the personal computer of fifteen years in the future, and Xerox never sold it as a product. In December 1979, Jobs negotiated visits to PARC for himself and Apple engineers in exchange for allowing Xerox to invest about a million dollars in pre-IPO Apple stock. Shown the graphical interface, Jobs later said, within ten minutes it was obvious to him that all computers would work this way someday. The visit became Silicon Valley most argued-over legend; the fair summary is that Apple took an unproductized research vision and spent five brutal years of original engineering making it real at consumer scale, inventing along the way now-universal conventions like overlapping windows that PARC systems handled differently, the menu bar, and drag-and-drop.

The first vehicle was the Lisa, a project begun in 1978 and aimed at business desktops. Jobs was forced off the Lisa team in 1980 by executives tired of his volatility, a demotion with enormous consequences, because he then seized a small research project started by computer scientist Jef Raskin, who envisioned an inexpensive, appliance-like computer for ordinary people, named Macintosh after his favorite apple variety, deliberately misspelled. Jobs took over the Macintosh team, pushed Raskin out by 1982, and remade the project in his own image: a graphical machine like the Lisa, but radically cheaper, built by a self-styled band of pirates flying a skull-and-crossbones flag over their building. The rivalry between the polished corporate Lisa team and the renegade Macintosh group became internal folklore, with Jobs openly telling Lisa engineers his cheaper machine would destroy theirs.

The Lisa shipped in January 1983 at 9,995 dollars, roughly 30,000 in later dollars, with a megabyte of memory, twin floppy drives, and a suite of seven integrated applications. It was a technical landmark, the first commercial personal computer with a graphical user interface and mouse, and it introduced ideas as basic as the desktop metaphor and document-centric files, but it was slow, expensive, and incompatible with everything, and corporate buyers were standardizing on the IBM PC. Lisa sold perhaps 10,000 units its first year against hopes ten times higher; renamed and repositioned repeatedly, it was dead by 1986, with thousands of unsold units eventually buried in a Utah landfill for the tax write-off, a burial that has become the emblem of magnificent commercial failure.

Meanwhile Apple needed a chief executive equal to a company now selling a billion dollars a year. In April 1983, Jobs completed a long courtship of John Sculley, the president of Pepsi-Cola, famed for the Pepsi Challenge marketing campaign, with one of the most quoted recruiting lines in business history: do you want to sell sugared water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world? Sculley came. For a year and a half, he and Jobs ran Apple in a much-advertised partnership, preparing the launch of the machine that would carry everything Lisa had pioneered to a price one quarter as high. The Macintosh was coming, and Apple intended to introduce it in a way no computer had ever been introduced.

sections.heading: 1984: The Macintosh Arrives
sections.body:
The Macintosh was announced to the world with sixty seconds of television. During the third quarter of Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, 1984, CBS aired a commercial directed by Ridley Scott, fresh from Blade Runner, that showed a gray auditorium of shaven-headed drones watching a Big Brother figure on a giant screen until a woman in athletic red and white, chased by helmeted police, hurled a sledgehammer through the face on the screen. The narration promised that on January 24th Apple Computer would introduce Macintosh, and that 1984 would not be like Nineteen Eighty-Four. The Orwell-inspired spot, produced by the agency Chiat Day for around 900,000 dollars with a similar amount in airtime, nearly did not run; Apple board hated it and ordered the airtime sold, but most could not be resold, and it aired once nationally. It generated millions of dollars of free news coverage, won the top advertising awards of the year, and permanently raised the ambitions of Super Bowl advertising. Two days later, at Apple annual shareholder meeting in the Flint Center in Cupertino, Jobs pulled the machine from a bag, inserted a floppy disk, and let the Macintosh introduce itself with synthesized speech, mocking IBM mainframes as it did.

The product itself was a compact beige all-in-one with a nine-inch black-and-white bitmapped display, 128 kilobytes of memory, a 3.5-inch floppy drive, a Motorola 68000 processor, and the mouse-driven graphical interface, priced at 2,495 dollars. It came with two applications, MacWrite and MacPaint, that demonstrated what the interface meant: proportional typefaces, pictures drawn freehand, cut and paste between programs, documents that looked on screen as they would on paper. Reviewers were dazzled by the experience and pointed at the weaknesses: 128K was far too little memory, there was no hard disk, the single floppy forced endless disk swapping, and almost no third-party software existed at launch. Initial sales were strong on curiosity, roughly 70,000 units in the first hundred days, then sagged badly through late 1984 and 1985 as business buyers stayed with IBM compatibles and the machine limitations bit. The 512K Fat Mac of September 1984 and the Mac Plus of 1986 progressively fixed the hardware.

What saved the Macintosh, and revealed its true market, was printing and page design. In 1985 Apple shipped the LaserWriter, one of the first affordable laser printers, built around Adobe PostScript page-description language; Aldus released PageMaker the same year; and the combination of Macintosh, LaserWriter, and PageMaker invented desktop publishing. For the first time, a small office could produce typeset-quality newsletters, advertisements, and books without a print shop; entire industries of graphic design, prepress, and publishing re-formed around the Mac, giving Apple a professional stronghold, in creative fields, that it never lost. The phrase what you see is what you get, WYSIWYG, moved from research jargon to selling point.

Inside Apple, however, 1985 was a year of collapse. The Macintosh sales miss collided with the ongoing IBM tide; the company endured its first quarterly loss and laid off about a fifth of its workforce. The Jobs and Sculley partnership curdled into open conflict over pricing, strategy, and authority, and when Jobs maneuvered to remove Sculley, the board sided with the CEO in May 1985, stripping Jobs of operating responsibility over the Macintosh division. That February, Wozniak had also departed day-to-day work, disillusioned. In September 1985, Jobs resigned as chairman, sold nearly all his shares, and left with a handful of colleagues to found a new computer company aimed at higher education, called NeXT. Apple sued, then settled. The founder era was over; the Macintosh, and the company, now belonged to professional management, and for several years that arrangement would look like a spectacular success.

sections.heading: The Sculley Years: Peak and Drift
sections.body:
The popular memory of Apple between Jobs departures compresses a decade into decline, but the late 1980s were in fact boom years. Under John Sculley, Apple raised Macintosh prices, rode the desktop publishing wave, and grew revenue from under 2 billion dollars in 1985 to 5.5 billion by 1990 and over 7 billion by 1992, with gross margins above 50 percent, among the fattest in the industry. The Macintosh II of 1987 brought color, expansion slots, and workstation-class power; the Macintosh SE and later the compact Classic served schools and homes; System software matured through the landmark System 7 of 1991, which added multitasking cooperative enough for the era, aliases, file sharing, and color throughout. In October 1991 Apple launched the PowerBook 100, 140, and 170, designed with Sony manufacturing help, which set the layout template every laptop still follows, palm rests with a centered trackball, and sold a billion dollars worth in their first year. Apple in this period was the largest personal computer maker in the world by revenue for a time, and its user base was famously the most loyal in the industry.

Sculley grandest personal bet was the Newton MessagePad, launched in August 1993, a handheld personal digital assistant, a term Sculley coined, with a stylus and handwriting recognition. The Newton was a genuine glimpse of the future, but its first-generation recognition failed often enough to become a national joke, lampooned in Doonesbury and on the Simpsons, and at 699 dollars and up it never found a mass market; the line improved substantially and sold modestly until it was killed in 1998. Its chip legacy mattered more than the product: Apple had co-founded ARM in 1990 with Acorn and VLSI to supply the Newton processor, and the eventual sale of that ARM stake helped keep Apple solvent in the late 1990s, while ARM descendants would one day power every iPhone.

The strategic catastrophe of the era was quieter: the failure to answer Microsoft. Windows 3.0 in 1990 and especially Windows 3.1 in 1992 brought a good-enough graphical interface to cheap commodity PCs from Compaq, Dell, and a hundred clone makers, machines whose prices fell relentlessly while Apple defended its margins. Apple had sued Microsoft in 1988 over the look and feel of Windows; the suit failed comprehensively by 1994, partly because Sculley 1985 agreement licensing certain interface elements for Windows 1.0 undercut it. Apple explored licensing Mac OS to other manufacturers in the late 1980s and repeatedly pulled back, protecting hardware margins in the short term while ceding the platform war in the long term. By the early 1990s the IBM-Microsoft-Intel standard owned business computing, and Apple worldwide market share was sliding from around 10 percent toward the low single digits.

Sculley responses grew grander and less focused. In 1991 Apple joined IBM and Motorola in the AIM alliance to build a new processor family, PowerPC, and spun up joint ventures, Taligent for a next-generation operating system and Kaleida for multimedia, that consumed hundreds of millions of dollars and shipped nothing of consequence. The PowerPC transition itself succeeded technically, with the first Power Macintoshes arriving in March 1994 and a clever emulator preserving old software, but the deeper problem remained: the classic Mac OS, brilliant in 1984, lacked the memory protection and true multitasking that modern systems required, and every internal project to replace it, culminating in the effort code-named Copland announced in 1994, would collapse under its own ambition. In June 1993, with margins compressing and the Newton bleeding money, the board removed Sculley in favor of the German-born operations chief Michael Spindler. Sculley decade had multiplied Apple revenue several times over, and had also spent, without solving, the two questions that would nearly kill the company: what replaces the Mac OS, and what does Apple sell when commodity PCs are good enough?

sections.heading: The Fall: Spindler, Amelio, and the Brink of Bankruptcy
sections.body:
The mid-1990s were the darkest stretch in Apple history, two chief executives and four years in which the company drifted to the edge of insolvency. Michael Spindler, who took over in June 1993, cut costs hard, laying off about 2,500 people, and made the decision Apple had debated for a decade: licensing Mac OS to clone manufacturers, beginning in 1995 with Power Computing, then Motorola, UMAX, and others. The theory was that clones would grow the Macintosh platform against Windows; the practice was that nimble cloners undercut Apple own high-margin hardware, cannibalizing the very profits that funded the platform, while adding barely any new users. The timing could not have been worse: Windows 95 launched in August 1995 with midnight store lines and a Rolling Stones soundtrack, closing most of the visible gap with the Mac experience, and that same year Apple catastrophically misforecast demand, first building the wrong products, then sitting on roughly a billion dollars of unsold inventory into 1996. The first quarter of 1996 brought a 69 million dollar loss and the board acted, replacing Spindler in February 1996 with director Gil Amelio, the semiconductor executive credited with turning around National Semiconductor.

Amelio inherited a company he later described as a ship with a hole in the bottom, and his crew argued about which direction to sail. He stabilized finances the blunt ways, raising cash, cutting the workforce by thousands, simplifying a product line that had metastasized into dozens of overlapping Performa, Quadra, and PowerBook models, but losses continued, 816 million dollars in fiscal 1996 and a staggering 1.045 billion in 1997. Quality problems dented the brand, including PowerBook 5300 units whose batteries could overheat. Market share fell below 4 percent, the stock hit a twelve-year low, and the business press wrote the company obituary on a weekly schedule; a 1996 Fortune cover story was titled simply The Fall of Apple, and in early 1997, Michael Dell, asked what he would do with Apple, answered that he would shut it down and give the money back to the shareholders. Both Sun Microsystems and IBM had explored acquiring Apple; the talks went nowhere.

The terminal problem remained the operating system. Copland, the in-house next-generation Mac OS, was formally cancelled in August 1996 after consuming years and perhaps half a billion dollars without ever approaching shippable quality, an engineering failure that left Apple with a 1984-lineage OS against Windows NT modern kernel. Amelio resolved to buy a replacement. Through late 1996 Apple evaluated candidates, most publicly Be Incorporated BeOS, built by former Apple executive Jean-Louis Gassee, whose price demands stalled the deal, as well as Windows NT itself and Sun Solaris. Then, in November, Steve Jobs called. His company NeXT had stopped making hardware in 1993 and survived selling NeXTSTEP, a polished, mature operating system with true memory protection, preemptive multitasking, and the best developer tools in the industry, built on a Unix foundation. On December 20, 1996, Apple announced it would acquire NeXT for approximately 429 million dollars in cash plus 1.5 million Apple shares, bringing NeXTSTEP in as the foundation of the future Mac OS, and bringing Steve Jobs back to the company he had co-founded, initially as an informal adviser to Amelio.

The advisership lasted six months. After a second quarter of heavy losses and a stock still scraping lows, the board, led by Edgar Woolard of DuPont, forced Amelio out in July 1997. Jobs, who had quietly placed allies and NeXT lieutenants, Avie Tevanian over software, Jon Rubinstein over hardware, into key posts, became de facto leader immediately and accepted the title of interim CEO in September 1997, a temporariness he maintained, half in jest, until dropping the interim in 2000. He took over a company with about ninety days of cash remaining. What happened next became the standard business-school case study in corporate resurrection.

sections.heading: The Return of Jobs and the Turnaround
sections.body:
Jobs moved with speed that shocked a demoralized company. In August 1997, at the Macworld Expo in Boston, he announced a peace treaty nobody expected: Microsoft would invest 150 million dollars in non-voting Apple stock, commit to five more years of Microsoft Office for the Mac, and settle the long-running patent disputes, with Internet Explorer becoming the Mac default browser. When Bill Gates appeared on the giant screen above him and the audience booed, Jobs delivered the line that defined the new realism: we have to let go of the notion that for Apple to win, Microsoft has to lose. The Office commitment mattered far more than the money; it told customers and developers the Mac would live. Jobs then executed the most famous product-line massacre in industry annals: reviewing dozens of overlapping products, he drew a two-by-two grid on a whiteboard, consumer and professional, desktop and portable, and killed everything that did not fit one of the four squares, including the Newton, the QuickTake camera, and some 70 percent of the roadmap. He terminated the clone licenses, buying out Power Computing key assets for about 100 million dollars, ending the margin bleed. Inventory, under a new operations executive named Tim Cook hired from Compaq in 1998, fell from months to days, as Cook outsourced manufacturing and rebuilt the supply chain into what would become the industry envy.

The cultural signal came in September 1997 with the Think Different advertising campaign from TBWA Chiat Day: black-and-white footage of Einstein, Gandhi, Picasso, Earhart, Dylan, and other heroes over a manifesto saluting the crazy ones, the misfits, the rebels. It sold no product; it re-sold the idea of Apple, to customers and, Jobs said pointedly, to Apple own employees. The financial turn was almost immediate: fiscal 1998 produced a 309 million dollar profit against the prior year billion-dollar loss.

The product that made the turnaround visible sat under a sheet until May 6, 1998. The iMac, designed by a previously obscure British designer named Jony Ive whom Jobs had elevated to lead design, was a translucent Bondi Blue all-in-one that looked like nothing else in an industry of beige boxes. Technically it was aggressive in both directions: it included fast Ethernet and a then-novel connector called USB, and it omitted the floppy drive entirely, a deletion widely mocked and quickly vindicated. The i stood, Apple said, for internet, and the iMac promise was two steps to get online. Shipped August 15, 1998, at 1,299 dollars, it sold about 800,000 units in less than five months, the fastest-selling Mac ever to that point, with a third of buyers new to the Mac; the 1999 five-flavor colored iMacs turned a computer into a fashion object. The consumer portable iBook followed in 1999, its clamshell design completing the two-by-two grid, along with the professional Power Mac G3 and G4 towers, one of which the US government briefly classified as a supercomputer for export purposes, a fact Apple advertised gleefully.

By 2000 the company was solidly profitable, its stock up many-fold from the 1997 trough, and Jobs dropped interim from his title at Macworld in January. The strategic groundwork for the next act was being laid in the same years: the NeXT-derived operating system was being rebuilt as Mac OS X, and in January 2001 Jobs articulated the digital hub strategy, the Mac as the center of an emerging lifestyle of digital cameras, camcorders, and music players. Two initiatives of 2001 would execute that strategy beyond anyone stated ambitions: a chain of retail stores, and a small white music player. The turnaround was complete; the transformation was about to begin.

sections.heading: Mac OS X and the Apple Stores
sections.body:
Two foundations of modern Apple were poured in the same two months of 2001, and both were widely predicted to fail. The first was Mac OS X, released on March 24, 2001, the payoff of the NeXT acquisition. Underneath, it was a different species from the classic Mac OS: a Unix-based core named Darwin, derived from NeXTSTEP Mach and BSD heritage, with protected memory and preemptive multitasking, meaning one crashing program could no longer take down the machine, the classic Mac most notorious flaw. On top sat the new Aqua interface, all translucency, shadows, and animation, with the Dock, and the developer frameworks from NeXT, Cocoa, that made Mac software dramatically faster to build. The transition was managed with unusual care: old applications ran in a Classic compatibility environment, and a Carbon framework let existing code be modernized incrementally. Early versions were sluggish and incomplete, 10.0 was fairly judged a public beta in all but name, but 10.1 that September and especially 10.2 Jaguar in 2002 made it fast and whole, and by the mid-2000s annual big-cat releases, Panther, Tiger, Leopard, were events developers queued for. OS X Unix foundations quietly changed Apple audience too, making Macs the default machine of programmers and scientists, and the same codebase, stripped and re-skinned, would later become the operating system of the iPhone, iPad, and Watch, making Mac OS X the ancestor of software now running on well over a billion devices.

The second foundation opened its doors on May 19, 2001, in Tysons Corner, Virginia, and Glendale, California: the first two Apple Stores. Conventional wisdom held that computer retail was a low-margin graveyard, Gateway own stores were failing as Apple opened, and a widely quoted BusinessWeek piece gave the effort two years before the pain set in. Jobs and retail chief Ron Johnson, hired from Target, had built something different from a computer shop: stores organized around activities rather than product boxes, machines all connected and usable, staff on salary rather than commission, and a support counter with a pretentious, memorable name, the Genius Bar. The bet was that people would not buy a premium, minority-platform computer sight unseen, but would if they could touch it and be taught; the stores were marketing, support, and distribution fused. They worked beyond argument: Apple retail reached a billion dollars in annual sales faster than any retailer in history to that date, and flagship stores, the glass cube on Fifth Avenue in New York, opened 2006, Regent Street in London, became civic landmarks. Within two decades there were over 500 stores across more than 25 countries, generating, by common estimate, the highest sales per square foot in world retail.

The stores and the OS reinforced the same strategy: control of the whole experience. Apple in the 2000s owned its operating system, designed its hardware, and now controlled the room where customers met both, the antithesis of the licensing-and-commodity logic that ruled the Windows PC world, and a model competitors from Microsoft to Samsung would later imitate with their own stores and integrated devices. One more 2001 product completed the digital hub tripod, announced that October between the two: a pocket-sized hard-disk music player. Together, OS X, the stores, and the iPod meant that a company which four years earlier had been ninety days from insolvency entered the new decade holding the software platform, the retail channel, and the consumer-electronics beachhead from which everything since has been launched.

sections.heading: The iPod and iTunes: A Thousand Songs in Your Pocket
sections.body:
On October 23, 2001, at a low-key event on the Cupertino campus weeks after the September 11 attacks, Jobs introduced a 399-dollar device the size of a deck of cards: the iPod, promising a thousand songs in your pocket. The pitch rested on two pieces of engineering: a new 1.8-inch Toshiba hard drive holding five gigabytes, which Apple hardware chief Jon Rubinstein had spotted on a Japan visit and locked up, and FireWire transfer, which loaded an album in seconds when USB rivals took an hour to fill. The scroll wheel, a design by Phil Schiller suggestion executed under Jony Ive, made navigating a thousand songs effortless. The product, developed in under a year by a team led by Tony Fadell, who had shopped the concept around the industry before Apple hired him, was greeted with skepticism, expensive, Mac-only, and a famous online comment dismissed it as no wireless, less space than a Nomad, lame. It sold steadily, then explosively: Windows compatibility arrived in 2002, and the iPod became the fastest-adopted consumer electronic device of its era, with the white earbuds a street-level status symbol and silhouette dancers on billboards worldwide.

The masterstroke was the store attached to it. Music piracy had exploded through Napster in 1999 and its successors, and the record industry answers were lawsuits and unusable subscription services. Jobs spent 2002 personally persuading the five major labels to try something nobody believed in: selling individual songs for 99 cents each, with rights terms uniform across labels, playable on unlimited iPods and burnable to CD. The iTunes Music Store opened on April 28, 2003, with 200,000 songs, and sold a million of them in six days, Jobs called it a turning point for the music industry, and it was, though not entirely the one the labels hoped for. The store broke the album bundle, retrained a pirating generation to pay for music, and made Apple, within a few years, the largest music retailer in the United States, passing Walmart in 2008. Career-long holdouts came aboard one by one, and the last symbolic capitulation, the Beatles catalog, arrived in 2010.

The iPod line then executed the product cadence that became the Apple playbook: relentless self-cannibalization. The iPod Mini of 2004, in anodized aluminum colors, was so popular it created shortages; Apple killed it at its peak in 2005 for the flash-memory Nano, thinner and tougher; the screenless Shuffle of 2005 took the entry price to 99 dollars; the video-capable fifth-generation iPod arrived the same year; and the App-Store-bearing iPod Touch of 2007 previewed the post-iPod world. The numbers redefined the company: iPod sales peaked near 55 million units in fiscal 2008, and at the height, iPod plus music revenue approached half of Apple total. Total cumulative sales exceeded 450 million units, making the iPod one of the best-selling consumer electronics products in history. Apple, still officially Apple Computer, had become the dominant company in an industry, portable music, that Sony Walkman lineage had owned for two decades; Sony, conflicted about piracy because it owned a record label and wedded to its proprietary formats, never effectively responded.

Strategically, the iPod decade taught Apple the lessons the iPhone would apply at ten times the scale. It proved Apple could manufacture and sell consumer electronics in the hundreds of millions through Tim Cook supply chain. It proved the halo effect: iPod owners walked into Apple Stores and walked out, in measurable numbers, with their first Macs, reversing decades of share decline. It proved the power of pairing a device with a content store that made honesty easier than piracy. And it hung a sword over the company own head that Jobs saw clearly: the device most likely to make the iPod obsolete was the mobile phone, because people would carry only one gadget. Rather than wait to be killed, Apple decided in 2004 to build the killer itself.

sections.heading: The iPhone: Reinventing the Phone
sections.body:
On January 9, 2007, at Macworld in San Francisco, Jobs delivered the most celebrated product introduction of the modern era. He teased three new devices, a widescreen iPod with touch controls, a revolutionary mobile phone, and a breakthrough internet communicator, repeated the trio until the audience caught on, and revealed they were one product: the iPhone. The announcement day, Apple Computer Inc. formally became Apple Inc., the computer no longer the point. The iPhone had been developed over two and a half years in extreme secrecy under the codename Project Purple, growing out of an experimental multitouch tablet effort that Jobs redirected at the phone first, on the logic that the phone was the device people would not leave home without. Two internal approaches had competed, an iPod-plus-phone with a click wheel, and a shrunken OS X with multitouch, championed by software chief Scott Forstall; the second won, an enormous engineering gamble that required fitting a desktop-class operating system into a pocket device. The contract with AT&T, then Cingular, was itself unprecedented: the carrier accepted a device it had never fully seen, surrendering all control over its software and interface, in exchange for exclusivity.

What shipped on June 29, 2007, at 499 and 599 dollars with a two-year contract, was recognizably the modern smartphone: a slab of glass, 3.5 inches of capacitive multitouch, no physical keyboard, no stylus, running real web pages in Safari, visual voicemail, and pinch-to-zoom photos. The industry incumbents laughed on the record. Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer predicted no significant market share; the BlackBerry maker and Nokia, then selling roughly four of every ten phones on Earth, judged a keyboardless touchscreen a niche toy. The first year had real weaknesses, 2G data speeds, no third-party apps, no copy and paste, and a 200-dollar price cut after two months that so angered early buyers Jobs issued store credit, but customers queued overnight anyway, and reviewers called it the Jesus phone with only partial irony. The iPhone 3G in 2008 fixed the network and added GPS; the 3GS, 4, and their successors settled into the annual cadence that reorganized the entire electronics industry calendar around one September event.

The consequences rank among the largest in business history. Nokia and BlackBerry, worth a combined fortune in 2007, were effectively destroyed within six years, Nokia handset business sold to Microsoft in 2013, BlackBerry reduced to a software brand. Google Android project, reoriented from a BlackBerry-like design the day the iPhone appeared, became the world volume operating system while Apple took the profit share, frequently above three quarters of global handset profits on a minority of unit sales. Adjacent industries reshaped or vanished: point-and-shoot cameras, portable GPS units, voice recorders, and eventually the iPod itself were absorbed into the slab. The iPhone became, by most accountings, the single most profitable product ever sold, cumulatively passing two billion units by the early 2020s and routinely generating half or more of Apple revenue.

Jobs closed the 2007 keynote with a Wayne Gretzky line about skating to where the puck is going, and the deeper point held: the iPhone was less a phone than a general-purpose computer that happened to make calls, and its full nature only emerged the following year, when Apple, reversing Jobs initial insistence that developers write web apps only, opened the device to third-party software. The App Store would turn the iPhone from a product into an economy, and it is the next chapter of the story.

sections.heading: The App Store, the iPad, and the Post-PC Era
sections.body:
The App Store opened on July 10, 2008, with about 500 applications, and rewrote the economics of software overnight. The terms were simple and, by the standards of prior software retail, generous: any registered developer could sell to every iPhone on Earth, Apple handled distribution, payment, and updates, and kept 30 percent. Within nine months the store passed a billion downloads; within a few years, millions of applications and hundreds of billions of cumulative downloads. Entire business categories were invented on it, ride-hailing, photo-sharing social networks, casual gaming empires, and the phrase there is an app for that, an Apple advertising line, entered the language and was trademarked. A genuine developer middle class emerged alongside spectacular fortunes; by the 2020s Apple was citing an app economy supporting millions of jobs, and cumulative developer payouts in the hundreds of billions of dollars. The store 30 percent commission and its status as the only gate onto the platform also seeded the antitrust wars of the following decade, from the Epic Games lawsuit filed in 2020 to the European Union Digital Markets Act, which by 2024 forced alternative app distribution in Europe.

The tablet Jobs had shelved in 2004 to build the phone returned on January 27, 2010, as the iPad, shipped that April 3 starting at 499 dollars. Reaction before launch was mockery about the name and the concept, a big iPhone; reaction after was 300,000 units sold the first day and about 15 million in nine months, the fastest-adopted consumer electronic product to that point. The iPad found the uses skeptics could not predict, replacing paper in cockpits and restaurants, becoming the default computer for children and grandparents, and anchoring creative work with the later Pencil, and it prompted Jobs most explicit statement of where computing was going. Standing before a slide of a truck at the D8 conference in 2010, he said PCs would become like trucks, still essential for some work, while most people would drive cars, meaning post-PC devices. Apple began describing itself as a mobile devices company; by 2011 the iPhone, iPad, and iPod together dwarfed the Mac, and the industry followed the puck.

The era carried a shadow. Jobs had been diagnosed in 2003 with a rare neuroendocrine pancreatic tumor; after surgery in 2004 and a liver transplant during a 2009 leave, he grew visibly gaunt through the iPad launch year. He took a third medical leave in January 2011, appeared twice more on stage that year, for the iPad 2 and the iCloud announcement, and resigned as CEO on August 24, 2011, writing that the day had come when he could no longer meet his own standard; Tim Cook, long the operational deputy, became CEO the same day. Jobs died at his Palo Alto home on October 5, 2011, at 56, the day after Apple announced the iPhone 4S. The mourning was global and strange for a corporate executive, flowers and apples with bites drawn on them piled outside Apple Stores from Shanghai to New York, and the Walter Isaacson biography published weeks later became one of the best-selling books of the year.

Jobs left a company transformed twice over, from wreck to juggernaut: in the quarter of his death Apple was the most valuable technology company on Earth, briefly the most valuable company of any kind, with the world reorganized around products, the Mac, iPod, iPhone, iPad, and the stores that sold them, none of which had existed in their current form when he returned in 1997. He also left a designated successor, a maturing executive bench, and an unannounced project, a watch, already stirring. The question asked everywhere that October, whether Apple could matter without its founder, would be answered by the least Jobs-like of his lieutenants, and answered, financially at least, beyond all argument.

sections.heading: The Cook Era: Services, Scale, and New Categories
sections.body:
Tim Cook, the Alabama-born operations master who had rebuilt Apple supply chain after 1998, was greeted by persistent skepticism: a logistics executive, the argument ran, could run but not grow Jobs company. The record answered otherwise. On Cook watch Apple revenue roughly quadrupled, from about 108 billion dollars in fiscal 2011 to a range around 380 to 400 billion in the mid-2020s, and its market value multiplied by more than an order of magnitude: Apple became the first American public company worth one trillion dollars on August 2, 2018, passed two trillion in August 2020, and touched three trillion first on January 3, 2022. Cook also reversed two Jobs doctrines without ceremony: Apple began paying dividends and buying back stock in 2012, ultimately returning more cash to shareholders than any company in history, and it embraced big-ticket acquisition once, buying Beats Electronics in 2014 for 3 billion dollars, gaining the headphone brand and the streaming service that became the seed of Apple Music.

The first new category of the era was the Apple Watch, announced September 2014 and shipped April 2015, initially marketed with fashion-house ambiguity, there was an 18-karat gold Edition, before finding its identity in fitness and health, heart-rate alerts, an FDA-cleared electrocardiogram in 2018, fall detection credited in recurring news stories with saving lives. Within a few years it outsold the entire Swiss watch industry in units. AirPods, the wireless earbuds launched December 2016 to mockery about lost toothbrush heads, became a cultural default and, by revenue, a business that alone would rank among large consumer electronics companies. The quieter revolution was silicon: beginning with the A4 chip in 2010, Apple built the world strongest consumer chip design team, and on November 10, 2020, it began replacing Intel processors in Macs with its own M1, an ARM-architecture descendant of the iPhone chips, delivering performance-per-watt the PC industry could not match; the two-year transition revitalized the Mac, which posted its best sales years ever immediately after.

The strategic pivot that defined the era was services. As iPhone unit growth flattened after 2015, peaking near 231 million units in fiscal 2015, Cook redirected Wall Street attention to the installed base, which passed two billion active devices, and the recurring revenue it generates: the App Store, iCloud storage, Apple Music from 2015, Apple Pay from 2014, AppleCare, and the 2019 subscription wave of TV Plus, Arcade, News Plus, and Fitness Plus, with an Oscar for the TV Plus film CODA in 2022 as cultural validation. Services revenue grew from about 8 billion dollars in fiscal 2011 to roughly 85 billion by fiscal 2023, approaching a quarter of revenue with margins near 70 percent, double the hardware business. Privacy became both conviction and competitive weapon, Cook refusing the FBI demand to weaken iPhone encryption in the 2016 San Bernardino case, and the 2021 App Tracking Transparency change reshaping the mobile advertising industry.

The era troubles were commensurate with its scale. Dependence on Chinese manufacturing and on the Chinese market became a geopolitical exposure, managed by slow diversification into India and Vietnam. Regulators on three continents attacked the App Store tollgate: the Epic litigation, the EU Digital Markets Act forcing sideloading in Europe from 2024, and a US Department of Justice antitrust suit filed in March 2024. The Vision Pro headset, announced June 2023 and shipped February 2, 2024, at 3,499 dollars, entered spatial computing to admiring reviews and modest sales, while critics noted Apple relative quiet in the generative artificial intelligence wave, answered from 2024 with the staged rollout of Apple Intelligence features. Through it all the company Jobs and Wozniak assembled from parts on credit remained, by most measures, the most profitable enterprise on Earth, earning roughly 100 billion dollars a year, its half-century arc, garage to three trillion, the reference story of the industry it helped invent.

sections.heading: Why Apple Mattered: Design, Integration, and Legacy
sections.body:
Stripped of the mythology, Apple historical importance rests on a handful of ideas it did not always originate but repeatedly proved at scale, and the first is that computers are consumer products, not institutional equipment. From the 1977 Apple II arriving in a friendly plastic case when rivals shipped kits, to the Macintosh insisting in 1984 that a computer should be learnable in an afternoon, to the iPhone putting a computer in two billion pockets, the through-line is the conviction that the person, not the machine or the systems administrator, is the customer. The industry vocabulary this created, the desktop, the mouse-driven interface popularized by the Mac, the app, the touchscreen phone, is now so universal it is hard to see as invention, which is the surest sign of influence: Apple competitors converged, sooner or later, on Apple template in personal computers, music players, phones, tablets, watches, and earbuds alike.

The second idea is integration. Through the industry commodity decades, when conventional wisdom held that value lay in horizontal layers, chips from one company, operating systems from another, boxes from a third, Apple stubbornly built the whole widget: its own hardware, its own software, eventually its own silicon and retail. The strategy nearly killed the company in the 1990s, when good-enough commodity PCs undercut it, and then became its unassailable moat in the mobile era, when battery life, smoothness, security, and design, virtues that live in the seams between hardware and software, decided the market. The M-series Mac chips of the 2020s are the argument in its final form: the company that once begged Motorola and Intel for competitive processors now designs the best ones in the industry for its own exclusive use. With integration came control, of the App Store, of repair, of what software may run where, and with control came the era defining fights over openness, from the 1990s clone wars to the Digital Markets Act; the tension between the polished walled garden and the open platform is Apple deepest legacy debate, and it is unresolved.

The third idea is that taste is an engineering discipline. Jobs, quoting himself, put it as the intersection of technology and the liberal arts; operationally it meant typography on the original Mac because Jobs had audited a calligraphy class, industrial design as a board-level function under Jony Ive, the removal of features, floppy drives, physical keyboards, headphone jacks, ahead of the market willingness, and marketing, from 1984 to Think Different to the silhouette dancers, treated as part of the product. The commercial results of the full system were unprecedented: the most profitable product line in history in the iPhone, the largest company by market value for most of a decade, over two billion devices in active use, and studied-everywhere case histories in both directions, the 1985 to 1997 decline as the standard cautionary tale about losing focus, the 1997 to 2011 resurrection as the standard playbook for recovering it.

The people themselves passed into folklore: Wozniak, the pure engineer who gave his designs away and left wealth on the table, still appearing at conferences as the hobbyist conscience of the industry; Jobs, the adopted college dropout whose exile and return supplied American business with its best redemption narrative, dead at 56 with his company at its zenith; Cook, the quiet operator who proved institutions can outgrow founders. Around them, a supporting cast, Markkula the investor-builder, Sculley the marketer who presided over both boom and drift, Ive the designer, Fadell the iPod builder, Forstall the software general, populates every serious history of the Valley. For a reference shelf, the essentials are the company own numbers, April 1, 1976, to the first three-trillion-dollar valuation on January 3, 2022, and the pattern beneath them: four times, with the Apple II, the Macintosh, the iPod, and the iPhone, one company reset the direction of the world largest industry, and it began with two friends, a garage that was really a bedroom, and a circuit board priced at 666.66 dollars.
